are the same for everyone. The solutions are visible: try first, then open
them.

## D1 · Count → share (question A)

**Goal.** Which island has the largest share of Adelie penguins? (Session 1,
slides 10 and 17.)

**Your turn.** Make a group and an outcome, then plot the share of each group
with the outcome, groups down the side.

```{r}
#| eval: false
d1_data <- penguins %>%
  mutate(
    group = ___,                       # the islands
    has_outcome = ___                  # TRUE when the penguin is Adelie
  )

ggplot(d1_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "___")
```

**Investigate.** What total does each bar divide by? Why can islands of
different sizes now be compared?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
d1_data <- penguins %>%
  mutate(
    group = island,
    has_outcome = species == "Adelie"
  )

ggplot(d1_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the island", y = NULL, fill = "Adelie")
```

Each bar divides by its own island's total (Biscoe 168, Dream 124,
Torgersen 52), so every bar runs from 0 to 1 and the unit "penguins" cancels.
Torgersen is 100% Adelie; Dream about 45%; Biscoe about 26%.
:::

### D1+ · Read and discuss: counties or people? (no code to write)

The same numbers can be counted per county or per person. `midwest` (built
into ggplot2) has one row per county in five Midwest states.

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
ggplot(midwest, aes(x = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  labs(x = "% below poverty", y = "Counties")

ggplot(midwest, aes(x = percbelowpoverty, weight = poptotal)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  labs(x = "% below poverty", y = "People")
```

**Talk.** The left plot counts counties; the right counts people. Why do they
look different? Which one answers "how many people live in poor counties?"
(This is choosing the unit, the same idea as choosing the total. Source:
ggplot2 book §5.2.)

## D2 · A summary with its spread

**Goal.** Show each species' rate of heavy penguins (over 4000 g) with its
standard error and its n. (Session 1, slides 13–16.)

**Your turn.** Finish the summary, then draw the rates with ±se.

```{r}
#| eval: false
d2_rates <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(body_mass_g) %>%
  mutate(has_outcome = body_mass_g > 4000) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    rate = mean(has_outcome),
    se = ___                           # the se of a rate
  )

ggplot(d2_rates, aes(x = rate, y = species,
                     xmin = rate - se, xmax = rate + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3)
```

**Investigate.** Whose range is widest? Look at its n and its rate.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
d2_rates <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(body_mass_g) %>%
  mutate(has_outcome = body_mass_g > 4000) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    rate = mean(has_outcome),
    se = sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / n)
  )
d2_rates

ggplot(d2_rates, aes(x = rate, y = species,
                     xmin = rate - se, xmax = rate + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Share heavier than 4000 g", y = NULL)
```

The se of a rate is `sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / n)`: it grows when n is small
and when the rate is near 0.5. Chinstrap has the smallest n, so its range is
wide; Gentoo's rate is close to 1, so its range is narrow even with a
similar n to Adelie.
:::

### D2b · A mean with its two spreads (Guided Project B2)

```{r}
d2b <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(flipper_length_mm) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(flipper_length_mm),
    sd = sd(flipper_length_mm),
    se = sd / sqrt(n)
  )
d2b
```

**Investigate.** Chinstrap's mean is about 5.9 mm above Adelie's. Big
compared to the se? Compared to the sd? (Session 2, slide 7.)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

Compared to the se (under 1 mm), 5.9 mm is large: we are confident the
means differ. Compared to the sd (about 6.5–7 mm), it is less than one sd:
many individual Adelie and Chinstrap penguins have similar flippers. Say
which comparison you mean.
:::

### D2+ · Optional: see the noise (resampling)

Redraw the penguins with replacement 200 times and compute each species'
rate again. The width of each cloud is the uncertainty the se describes.
(`map()` and `slice_sample()` are new; read and run, no need to write them.)

```{r}
resamples <- map(1:200, \(i) {
  penguins %>%
    drop_na(body_mass_g) %>%
    slice_sample(prop = 1, replace = TRUE) %>%
    group_by(species) %>%
    summarize(rate = mean(body_mass_g > 4000))
}) %>%
  bind_rows(.id = "draw")

ggplot(resamples, aes(x = rate, y = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  labs(x = "Rate in each of 200 redraws", y = NULL)
```

**Talk.** Which species' cloud is widest? Does that match D2's ranges?

## D3 · Zoom or filter?

**Goal.** See what a zoomed axis does to bars, and compute its Lie Factor.
(Session 2, slides 4–7.)

**Your turn.** Zoom the counts so the view starts at 40, then filter with
the same limits.

```{r}
#| eval: false
d3_counts <- ggplot(penguins, aes(y = island)) +
  geom_bar()

d3_counts + ___(xlim = c(40, 175), expand = FALSE)   # zoom
d3_counts + ___(limits = c(40, 175))                 # filter
```

**Investigate.** Compute the Lie Factor of the zoomed plot for Biscoe (168)
vs Torgersen (52).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
d3_counts <- ggplot(penguins, aes(y = island)) +
  geom_bar()

d3_counts + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(40, 175), expand = FALSE)
d3_counts + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(40, 175))
```

```{r}
drawn_ratio <- (168 - 40) / (52 - 40)
data_ratio <- 168 / 52
drawn_ratio / data_ratio
```

The zoom keeps all the data but cuts the bars at 40: Biscoe looks about 10.7
times longer than Torgersen, while the counts differ 3.2 times, a Lie Factor
of about 3.3. The filter removes the bars, because every bar starts at 0,
outside the limits. Bars start at 0; to look closer, use points and say so.
:::

### D3+ · Compared to what? A narrow time window

`economics` (built into ggplot2) has monthly US data from 1967 to 2015.

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
economics %>%
  filter(date >= as.Date("2000-01-01"), date < as.Date("2008-01-01")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = unemploy / pop)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Unemployed per person, 2000–2007")

ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy / pop)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Unemployed per person, 1967–2015")
```

**Talk.** What story does the left plot tell on its own? What does the full
series add? Why divide by `pop`? (Tufte's "compared to what?" and
standardized units, 2001, p. 77.)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

The 2000–2007 window shows a rise and a fall that look dramatic; the full
series shows they are small next to the peaks of the early 1980s and 2009.
Dividing by the population makes years comparable: the number unemployed
grows partly because the population grows.
:::

## D4 · Change the frame

**Goal.** Ask question B (of all Adelie, what share lives on each island?)
and compare the frames. (Session 1, slide 17; Session 2, slides 9–11.)

**Your turn.** Keep the Adelie, count per island, and turn the counts into
shares of all Adelie. Draw them sideways.

```{r}
#| eval: false
d4_shares <- penguins %>%
  filter(species == "Adelie") %>%
  count(island) %>%
  mutate(share = ___)

ggplot(d4_shares, aes(x = share, y = island)) +
  geom_col()
```

**Investigate.** D1 said Torgersen is the "most Adelie" island. Does D4 agree?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
d4_shares <- penguins %>%
  filter(species == "Adelie") %>%
  count(island) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))
d4_shares

ggplot(d4_shares, aes(x = share, y = island)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Share of all Adelie", y = NULL)
```

No: of all 152 Adelie, Dream holds the largest share (about 37%), Torgersen
34%, Biscoe 29%. Question A (÷ island total) and question B (÷ Adelie total)
answer different questions; say which one you mean.
:::

### D4+ · Bar or pie?

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
p_share <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = "all", fill = species)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of all penguins")
p_share
p_share + coord_polar(theta = "y")
```

**Talk.** Adelie (44%) or Gentoo (36%): which is easier to compare on the
bar, and on the pie? Why? (Tufte, 2001, p. 77: don't show more dimensions
than the data have.)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

On the bar, both are lengths on one scale from 0 to 1, easy to compare. On
the pie, you compare angles and areas, which people judge less accurately,
especially when slices are close. The data have one dimension (a share per
species); the pie spreads it over angle and area: more work for the reader,
and no new information. Prefer the bar.
:::

---

*Data:* Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. (2020). *palmerpenguins:
Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data* (R package). `midwest` and
`economics` come with ggplot2 (Wickham, Navarro & Pedersen, *ggplot2*, 3rd
ed.).
